transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I suppose what brings me in is... I keep hearing these very clear voices. Mostly in my apartment, but also sometimes when I visit the museum, especially in the empty rooms. It sounds just like women whispering from right behind the walls, and they keep telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. 

I actually used to take quite a few photographs myself, back after I finished my degree. Mostly black and white architecture shots. I had this wonderful little darkroom set up in my basement before the pipes burst in the late nineties. Water just gets right into the drywall and you can never really get the mildew smell out, no matter what you do. I tried using bleach, but my sister swore by white vinegar. She always had the strangest cleaning tips, though she never did learn how to properly organize a photo album... anyway, she moved to Florida a few years ago. The humidity there is terrible for paper goods. But yes, the women whispering in the walls about the archives, they are just so loud lately.
Have you had a period of several days or longer when you felt unusually high, energized, or irritable?

Oh, yes, there are stretches of days like that. I get these days when I feel just... radiant. Like I've been chosen for something incredibly important. I have all these brilliant plans, you see, and I feel so awake. But then, if someone questions my plan or tells me to slow down, I become furious. It feels exactly as if they are trying to erase me. 

Like the cashier at the art supply store the other day. I was buying archival pens, the ones with the very fine felt tips, and she told me I was moving too fast and holding up the line. I was just trying to explain the ink viscosity to her! You know, India ink is really the only way to go if you want something to last on paper. My grandfather used to write all his letters in India ink. He had this beautiful, heavy brass inkwell on his desk. I used to polish it for him on Sundays when I was a little girl. The polish smelled a bit like lemons, but chemical, you know? Not like real lemons. Real lemons are so terribly expensive now anyway, I saw them for over a dollar each at the market last week. I can't imagine paying that just for a garnish. 

But yes, the anger. I get very, very angry when people try to get in my way or erase my work during those radiant days.
During those radiant periods, do you need much less sleep than usual?

Oh, sleep... yes, sleep becomes quite unnecessary. During those times, I only need maybe two or three hours. I'll wake up long before dawn, and I just feel completely ready to go. I tell myself that sleep is really only for people who don't have an archive to rescue. 

You know, dawn is actually the best time for natural light photography, anyway. The 'golden hour,' they call it. Though really, there are two golden hours, one in the morning and one right before sunset. The morning light always feels a bit cooler to me, a bit more crisp. I used to try to capture the frost on the wrought-iron fences in my old neighborhood during that morning golden hour. Wrought iron is so fascinating, isn't it? The way they twist the metal. They don't make fences like that anymore. Now it's all chain link or that terrible vinyl fencing that cracks in the winter. My neighbor put up a vinyl fence and it looked dreadful after just one season. She had this little yappy dog, a Pomeranian, I think, that would just hurl itself at the vinyl panels all day long. Such a nervous little creature. But yes, I wake up so early and I just don't need the rest at all.
Have you ever heard the voices when you were not having one of those energized or radiant periods?

Well, yes... yes, I do. Actually, there was a stretch... oh, maybe a few weeks? Where I wasn't feeling radiant at all. I wasn't energized, I wasn't feeling grand or important. But the whispers were still there in the apartment. And I was absolutely certain those arts people were monitoring my phone. 

They can do that now, you know. The technology is just everywhere. I remember reading an article in a magazine at the dentist's office about how smartphones are always listening to you. The dentist I used to go to, Dr. Aris, he had the most wonderful waiting room. He kept a saltwater aquarium right in the center, full of these beautiful, brightly colored fish. Tangs and clownfish. Saltwater tanks are incredibly difficult to maintain, the salinity has to be absolutely perfect or the fish get stressed. I tried keeping a freshwater tank once, just some guppies and a neon tetra, but the filter kept getting clogged with algae. Algae is so persistent. You can scrub the glass, but it always comes back if the tank is near a window. I had mine near the east-facing window in the living room, which was lovely for the morning light, but terrible for the algae. 

But yes, even when I wasn't feeling all that energy, I could still hear them whispering, and I just knew my phone wasn't safe.
Have these voices and beliefs been going on for at least six months?

Well, let me think... yes, it's been longer than six months. I'd say the voices and that absolute certainty that people are watching my archive... it's been going on for about eight months now. 

Eight months... so that would mean it started right around the time the leaves were turning. I've always loved the autumn foliage. There's this one enormous Japanese maple in the botanical gardens that turns the most brilliant, violent shade of crimson. I used to try and sketch it, but colored pencils never quite capture the depth of that red. You really need a good watercolor for that, maybe an alizarin crimson mixed with just a touch of burnt umber. Watercolors are so unforgiving, though. If you make a mistake, you can't just paint over it like you can with oils. My college roommate, Brenda, she was an oil painter. She used turpentine to clean her brushes, and our little dorm room always smelled like pine and harsh chemicals. It gave me dreadful headaches, but she refused to switch to a less toxic solvent. She ended up moving to New Mexico, I think, for the light. Everyone says the light in Taos is spectacular for painting. The desert air does something to the way the sun scatters, no humidity to get in the way. 

But yes... what were we saying? Oh, right, the whispering and the watching. About eight months of that, yes.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt very depressed or lost interest or pleasure in most things?

Well, yes... yes, there are times like that. There are these long stretches where everything just feels heavy and gray. I'll just sit at my kitchen table for hours... not doing anything, really. I let my little herb pots dry out completely. I had basil and thyme, and a beautiful rosemary bush. Rosemary is so wonderful for roasting chicken, isn't it? You just tuck a few sprigs under the skin with some lemon and garlic, and it smells heavenly while it cooks. My mother used to make roast chicken every Sunday. We'd always have it with mashed potatoes and those little tiny green peas. I never liked the peas, they were always too mushy, but she insisted we eat them. She said they were good for our eyesight, though I think she was confusing them with carrots. Carrots have beta-carotene, you know. That's what gives them that bright orange color. 

But yes, during those heavy stretches, I don't call any of my friends back. I just can't bring myself to pick up the phone. And I don't feel any interest in anything, not even when someone invites me to a concert or a gallery opening. And I used to love gallery openings... the cheap wine in those little plastic cups, the cheese cubes on toothpicks...
Have the voices or the belief that people are watching your archive ever happened when you were not also feeling depressed or unusually energized?

Well, yes, I think I mentioned that a little bit ago, didn't I? There was that stretch of several weeks. I wasn't feeling grand or full of that buzzing energy, and I wasn't in one of those heavy, gray slumps either. I was just... ordinary. Doing my laundry, making my tea. But the whispers were still there in the apartment. They didn't stop. And I was still entirely convinced those arts people were monitoring my phone. 

It's just so violating, having your phone listened to. I really miss the old landlines. We had a canary yellow one in the kitchen when I was growing up. The cord was so long you could stretch it all the way into the dining room, around the doorframe, if you wanted a little privacy. My mother used to get it all tangled up into knots. She'd talk to her sister Maureen for hours on a Sunday. Aunt Maureen lived in Chicago, and she made the most incredible deep-dish pizza. She sent us the recipe once on a little floral index card, but it got lost when we moved to the new house. Moving is such a nightmare, isn't it? All those cardboard boxes. The packing tape always gets stuck to your fingers and leaves that awful sticky residue that you have to scrub off with rubbing alcohol. Rubbing alcohol has such a sharp smell, it always reminds me of the nurse's office in middle school. 

But yes, even when my mood was perfectly fine, not high and not low, the whispers and the phone monitoring were still happening.
Have you had any recent head injury, new medical illness, or started any new medications or substances around the time these symptoms began?

No, no head injuries. I've always been very sure-footed. You have to be careful, though, especially with those uneven brick sidewalks over by the historic district. They look charming, but the oak tree roots have pushed all the bricks up at these terrible, jagged angles. My old neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she tripped on one of those bricks a few years ago and broke her wrist. She had to wear this awful fiberglass cast for six weeks. It was bright purple. She said her granddaughter picked the color. Kids love those bright, neon colors, don't they? 

When I was a girl, everything was much more muted. Pastels, mostly. I had a lovely Easter dress once that was the exact color of a robin's egg, with little white lace around the collar. My mother made it herself on her Singer sewing machine. The foot pedal made this rhythmic clicking sound... click, clack, click, clack. It was almost hypnotic. She used to let me sort her button tin while she sewed. So many buttons in there... mother-of-pearl, heavy brass ones from old military coats, little wooden toggles. I'd arrange them all by size on the living room rug. 

But what were you asking? Oh, no, I haven't been sick with anything new. And I don't take any drugs or new medications, just my regular daily vitamin. So nothing like that, no.
Have you ever had a period when your mood was so elevated or irritable that you were hospitalized or unable to function normally?

Well, yes, there are times... there are these days where I just feel absolutely radiant. Like I'm glowing from the inside out, and I feel so completely chosen, you know? Like I have this incredible, grand purpose. I'll have these brilliant plans, just so much energy buzzing through me. I'll stay up all night organizing my files and writing down these incredible ideas. I used to write everything down in those little marbled composition notebooks. The ones with the black and white covers? They always remind me of elementary school. We had to use those for our spelling tests. I was an excellent speller. I won the spelling bee in fifth grade with the word "chrysanthemum." It's such a lovely flower, isn't it? The deep burgundy ones are my favorite, they look so rich against the autumn leaves. I used to love pressing autumn leaves in heavy books. The encyclopedias were the best for that. We had a whole set of Encyclopedia Britannica, bound in that dark blue leather with the gold lettering on the spine... 

Oh, but you asked about the mood... yes, when I'm feeling that radiant, chosen way, if someone tries to tell me to slow down, or if they question my plans, I get furious. Just absolutely enraged. It feels like they're trying to erase me, to stamp out this beautiful, important thing I'm doing. It gets so intense that, well, yes, there was a time they had to take me to the hospital because I just couldn't function in the normal way anymore. I was too wrapped up in my purpose, and I was so angry at everyone trying to stop me.
Have there ever been at least two weeks when the voices or the belief that people were watching you continued even though you were not having any mood symptoms at all?

Yes, I... I thought we just talked about that a little while ago. But yes, there was a stretch of several weeks. I wasn't feeling grand, I didn't have that buzzing energy, and I wasn't feeling low either. I was just normal. But the whispers were still there in the apartment, and I was still absolutely certain those arts people were monitoring my phone. 

It's so strange how time works, isn't it? Weeks can feel like days, or days can stretch out forever. My grandfather had this beautiful antique grandfather clock in his hallway. It chimed every quarter hour. The sound was so deep and resonant, you could feel it in your chest if you stood close enough. He used to wind it every Sunday morning with this heavy brass key. He kept the key in a little wooden box lined with green velvet. Green velvet always reminds me of Christmas dresses. I had one with a white lace collar... or did I mention the lace collar already? It might have been the Easter dress. Oh, the Easter dress was blue. Like a robin's egg. 

But yes, to answer your question, those weeks went by, my mood was perfectly fine, not high or low, but the whispers and the phone monitoring didn't stop at all.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when the voices or the belief that people were watching you continued even though you were not having any mood symptoms at all?

I... I feel like we just went over this, didn't we? But yes, I can tell you again. There was a time, it went on for several weeks, actually. I wasn't feeling grand or special, and I didn't have all that buzzing energy, but I wasn't sad either. My mood was just... flat. Normal, I suppose. But the whispers in the apartment, they didn't stop. And I was still completely sure those arts people were listening in on my phone calls. 

Telephones used to be so different, didn't they? We had a rotary phone when I was little. It was a heavy, black thing that sat on a little table in the hallway. You had to stick your finger in the holes and pull the dial all the way around. It made this very satisfying *shhh-click, shhh-click* sound. My mother had this long, coiled cord attached to the receiver so she could walk into the kitchen while she talked to her sister, Aunt Clara. Aunt Clara made the most wonderful rhubarb pie. She grew the rhubarb right in her own backyard. The leaves are poisonous, you know, you can only eat the stalks. They look a bit like red celery. I always thought celery was such a boring vegetable, unless you put peanut butter on it. We used to call it "ants on a log" when we put raisins on top of the peanut butter. 

But yes, like I said, the mood was fine for those weeks, but the voices and the phone monitoring... that just kept right on going.
Have there ever been any times when the voices or the belief that your phone was being monitored were present while you were not having any mood symptoms at all for at least two weeks?

Doctor, are you sure you're feeling quite alright? I'm starting to worry about your memory. You've asked me this exact same thing three times now! It feels like a broken record in here. 

Do you know what a broken record actually sounds like? People say the phrase all the time, but nobody listens to vinyl anymore. My father had a beautiful mahogany record player console in our living room when I was growing up. It was huge, took up half the wall. We used to listen to Nat King Cole on Sunday evenings. He had such a smooth voice, like melted butter. I tried making homemade butter once, actually, in a glass mason jar. You just shake heavy cream until your arms absolutely ache. It takes ages. My arms were so sore the next day I could barely lift my teacup. I collect teacups, you know. Bone china is the best, it's so delicate you can almost see right through it if you hold it up to the light. I have one with little hand-painted violets on it that I found at an estate sale...

But yes, to answer you again, there was a period of several weeks where I wasn't especially energized or grand at all, my mood was just completely normal, but I still heard the whispers in the apartment and I remained totally convinced the arts people were monitoring my phone. Do you want me to write it down for your notes this time?
Over the entire eight months, would you say the times with depression or the high, energized mood have been present for most of the illness, or only for a smaller part of it?

Oh, definitely most of it. Most of these months since I retired have been completely dominated by these long stretches of feeling... well, just so driven. Like I have been chosen for something, and I get so irritable because I am just completely unable to slow down. Even when I was also having some of those quieter, withdrawn days, that high energy was taking up the vast majority of the time. 

I really thought retirement was supposed to be relaxing, you know? My neighbor, Susan, she retired last year and immediately took up knitting. She sits on her front porch all day making these enormous, hideous afghans. She made me one for Christmas. It was mustard yellow and this awful burnt orange color. Who puts those colors together? It reminded me of the carpet in my first apartment back in the late seventies. Shag carpet was absolutely everywhere back then. You had to buy a special plastic rake just to keep it looking fluffy. Can you imagine? Raking your living room floor! My roommate at the time had a little tabby cat that would lose its toy mice in that carpet for weeks at a time. We would step on them in the middle of the night and nearly break our necks on the way to the bathroom. The bathroom had pink tiles. I always hated pink...
Have there been any times when the voices or the belief that people were watching you were present while you were having no mood symptoms at all?

Doctor, I really... I don't know what to say. Are you playing a trick on me? Is this some sort of memory test for *you*? We just talked about this. I've told you three times now. 

Yes, there was a period of several weeks where I wasn't feeling grand or energized at all. My mood was completely normal. But I still heard the whispers in the apartment, and I was still absolutely certain those arts people were monitoring my phone. 

I'm starting to think maybe you need to be evaluated. My cousin Harold had a terrible memory toward the end. He couldn't remember where he put his keys, his glasses, his own dog! It was a lovely Golden Retriever named Buster. Buster used to shed everywhere. You'd sit on Harold's sofa and stand up looking like you were wearing a fur coat. I've never been fond of fur coats. They seem so old-fashioned now, don't they? Plus, the upkeep is just tremendous. You have to put them in cold storage during the summer. I knew a woman who kept her mink in her deep freezer next to the frozen peas. Can you imagine reaching for a bag of peas and grabbing a dead mink instead? I prefer fresh peas, anyway. If you shell them yourself, they're so sweet. You can just pop them right in your mouth like candy...

But yes, doctor, for the fourth time, the voices and the phone monitoring were still there even when my mood was completely fine for several weeks. Please, write it down this time.
During your elevated or depressed mood episodes, do the voices or the belief that your phone is being monitored get noticeably worse?

Well, yes, they absolutely do. When I get into those states where I'm barely sleeping—maybe two or three hours a night—and I'm just racing around from one archive task to another, sorting everything... that's when it all gets so intense. I hear those women's voices so clearly then, and I just know, without a shadow of a doubt, that the museum board is tracking my work. They want to steal my research, I'm sure of it. 

I used to love going to museums when I was younger. The Natural History Museum was my favorite. They had this massive blue whale suspended from the ceiling. It was just breathtaking. I always wondered how they dusted something that large. Do they use a giant feather duster on a huge pole? Or maybe scaffolding? I hired a man to clean my gutters once, and he brought this incredibly tall ladder. He was so high up, it made my stomach drop just watching him. I offered him a glass of lemonade when he came down, but he said he preferred iced tea. I make a wonderful sun tea in the summer. You just put the tea bags in a big glass pitcher and leave it out on the patio table all afternoon. The sun does all the work. My grandmother taught me how to do that. She always served it with fresh mint from her garden. Her garden was spectacular—she had these prize-winning peonies that were the size of dinner plates... 

But yes, when I'm in one of those high-energy stretches, the voices and the feeling of being watched by the board definitely flare up right alongside it.
Have you ever had a time when your mood was so elevated or irritable that it caused major problems in your life, like needing hospitalization or making you unable to function normally?

Well, it certainly made a mess of things, if I'm being honest. I completely lost the trust of my colleagues, and I was missing my board meetings... and my bills, too. The bills just piled up on the kitchen counter for weeks. I usually keep them in this lovely little wicker basket I bought at a craft fair in Vermont years ago. Vermont is just so beautiful in the autumn. The leaves turn these incredible shades of red and gold. We used to take driving tours up Route 100, stopping at all the little country stores to buy maple syrup. Real maple syrup, mind you, not that artificial corn syrup nonsense they sell in the plastic bottles at the grocery store. It makes such a difference on pancakes. I used to make blueberry pancakes from scratch every Sunday morning. You have to use fresh blueberries, though, the frozen ones make the batter turn a dreadful shade of gray... 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the problems. Things got so out of hand that my cousin and one of the museum administrators actually had to step in. I just couldn't manage my appointments or handle my money safely on my own anymore, let alone go to public events. The administrator, a rather stern woman named Beatrice, she wore these sensible orthopedic shoes. They squeaked on the linoleum floors at the museum. Squeak, squeak, squeak. It drove me absolutely up the wall. Have you ever tried to concentrate with a squeaky shoe in the room? It's like a dripping faucet. I had a plumber come fix my bathroom sink last month because of a drip, and he charged me an absolute fortune just to replace a tiny rubber washer... but yes, they had to take over my affairs because I just couldn't function safely on my own during all of that.
Have there been any periods when the voices or the belief that people were watching you were present while your mood was normal?

Doctor, I... we just talked about this. I know we did. Are you feeling alright? You're asking me the exact same thing again. I'm really starting to worry about your memory. My cousin Harold, bless his heart, started out just like this. Asking the same questions over and over. "Did you feed the dog?" he'd say. "Yes, Harold, I fed Buster." Five minutes later, "Did you feed the dog?" Buster was getting quite plump toward the end because Harold kept feeding him, forgetting he'd already done it. Golden Retrievers will eat anything you put in front of them, you know. They have absolutely no self-control. I once saw Buster eat an entire stick of butter that Harold left on the coffee table. The mess on the rug afterward... well, I won't go into details, but it required a professional carpet cleaner. I used a lovely company called Steamer's Choice. The young man who came out was so polite, he even took his shoes off at the door without me having to ask. It's so rare to find good manners these days, don't you think? Young people are always staring at their little screens, walking right into traffic...

But yes, doctor, as I said before, there was a stretch of several weeks where I wasn't energized or feeling grand at all. My mood was perfectly normal. But the whispers in my apartment were still there, and I was still completely convinced those arts people were monitoring my phone. Please, make a note of it this time so we don't have to go over it again.
Have you ever had a period of at least one week when your mood was clearly elevated or irritable with unusually high energy, but there were no voices or paranoid beliefs at all?

Well, no, I don't think so. It seems like whenever I've had those times where I'm just bursting with energy and staying up all night, the voices and the feeling that the museum board is watching me are always right there with it. I can't think of a time when I was all revved up like that but didn't have the whispers or the paranoia. It all seems to happen together. 

It reminds me of how my grandmother's arthritis would always act up right before a thunderstorm. She'd be sitting in her rocking chair, knitting—she made the most beautiful afghans, all these intricate cable patterns in deep hunter greens and burgundy reds. I still have one draped over the back of my sofa. Anyway, she'd rub her knuckles and say, "A storm's brewing, I can feel it in my bones." And sure enough, within a few hours, the sky would turn that strange bruised purple color, and the thunder would start rolling in. I've always loved thunderstorms, provided I'm safe inside with a cup of tea, of course. There's something so cozy about listening to the rain lash against the windowpanes while you're wrapped up in a warm blanket. I used to have a cat, a big fluffy Maine Coon named Barnaby, who would hide under the bed at the first clap of thunder. He was terrified of loud noises. Even the vacuum cleaner sent him scurrying. I had to buy one of those silent sweepers just to keep the rugs tidy without traumatizing the poor dear...

But to answer your question, no, I've never had that high energy without the other things happening too. They're always a package deal, unfortunately.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when the voices or paranoid beliefs continued while you were not having any mood symptoms at all?

Doctor, I really must insist you get your hearing checked, or perhaps buy a new pen, because we literally just went over this! Are you playing some sort of trick on me? As I said just a moment ago, yes, there was a period of several weeks where I wasn't especially energized or grand at all. My mood was completely fine. But I still heard the whispers in my apartment, and I remained entirely convinced those arts people were monitoring my phone. 

Speaking of phones, did you know they don't even make rotary phones anymore? I used to have a beautiful avocado green rotary phone mounted on the wall in my kitchen. It had such a satisfying heft to the receiver. You could really slam it down if a telemarketer was being rude. Now it's all just tapping on pieces of glass. My niece bought me one of those smartphones, and the screen is always covered in smudges. I try to wipe it with my microfiber cloth—the yellow one, mind you, not the blue one. The blue one is strictly for dusting the porcelain figurines. I have a lovely collection of Lladro figurines in my sitting room. The little girl holding the basket of spring flowers is my absolute favorite. I bought her at an estate sale back in, oh, it must have been 1988. The woman running the sale was wearing the most dreadful floral muumuu, it looked exactly like a couch from the 1970s... 

But honestly, doctor, please write it down this time. Several weeks. No mood issues. Still hearing the whispers and knowing the arts people were on the phone. Do you have it now?
Have you ever had any hallucinations or paranoid beliefs when you were not having any mood symptoms at all?

Doctor, I... I am genuinely starting to wonder if you are listening to a single word I say. We have gone over this three times now! Are you writing any of this down? You're looking right at me, but I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, has a brick wall in her backyard, right along the property line. It’s covered in ivy. English ivy, I believe. It looks very picturesque in the spring, but it is an absolute nightmare to maintain. The roots dig right into the mortar and ruin the structural integrity. I told her, "Mildred, that ivy is going to pull your wall down one day," but she just waved me off. She’s terribly stubborn, Mildred is. She insists on wearing open-toed sandals well into November, even when there's frost on the ground. I suppose some people just refuse to listen to reason, much like you refusing to remember what I just told you!

But fine, I will say it one more time, and please, I beg of you, commit it to memory. Yes, there was a period of several weeks where I felt completely normal—not grand, not overly energized, just my regular self. But during that time, the whispers in my apartment were still there, clear as day, and I was still absolutely certain that those arts people were monitoring my phone calls. I don't know how else to explain it to you, doctor. Do I need to write it on a sticky note and put it on your forehead?

doctor.intent: To open the interview and learn the patient's chief concern.
doctor.question: Hello, I'm Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep hearing clear voices in my apartment and sometimes in empty museum rooms, like women whispering from behind the walls telling me which photographs belong in the archive.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the item corresponding to the chief_complaint_symptom_code, which is S020.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, I suppose what brings me in is... I keep hearing these very clear voices. Mostly in my apartment, but also sometimes when I visit the museum, especially in the empty rooms. It sounds just like women whispering from right behind the walls, and they keep telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. 

I actually used to take quite a few photographs myself, back after I finished my degree. Mostly black and white architecture shots. I had this wonderful little darkroom set up in my basement before the pipes burst in the late nineties. Water just gets right into the drywall and you can never really get the mildew smell out, no matter what you do. I tried using bleach, but my sister swore by white vinegar. She always had the strangest cleaning tips, though she never did learn how to properly organize a photo album... anyway, she moved to Florida a few years ago. My cousin Harold, bless his heart, started out just like this. Asking the same questions over and over. "Did you feed the dog?" he'd say. "Yes, Harold, I fed Buster." Five minutes later, "Did you feed the dog?" Buster was getting quite plump toward the end because Harold kept feeding him, forgetting he'd already done it. Golden Retrievers will eat anything you put in front of them, you know. They have absolutely no self-control. I once saw Buster eat an entire stick of butter that Harold left on the coffee table. The mess on the rug afterward... well, I won't go into details, but it required a professional carpet cleaner. I used a lovely company called Steamer's Choice. The young man who came out was so polite, he even took his shoes off at the door without me having to ask. It's so rare to find good manners these days, don't you think? Young people are always staring at their little screens, walking right into traffic...

But yes, doctor, as I said before, there was a stretch of several weeks where I wasn't energized or feeling grand at all. My mood was perfectly normal. But the whispers in my apartment were still there, and I was still completely convinced those arts people were monitoring my phone. Please, make a note of it this time so we don't have to go over it again.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I don't think so. It seems like whenever I've had those times where I'm just bursting with energy and staying up all night, the voices and the feeling that the museum board is watching me are always right there with it. I can't think of a time when I was all revved up like that but didn't have the whispers or the paranoia. It all seems to happen together. 

It reminds me of how my grandmother's arthritis would always act up right before a thunderstorm. She'd be sitting in her rocking chair, knitting—she made the most beautiful afghans, all these intricate cable patterns in deep hunter greens and burgundy reds. I still have one draped over the back of my sofa. Anyway, she'd rub her knuckles and say, "A storm's brewing, I can feel it in my bones." And sure enough, within a few hours, the sky would turn that strange bruised purple color, and the thunder would start rolling in. I've always loved thunderstorms, provided I'm safe inside with a cup of tea, of course. There's something so cozy about listening to the rain lash against the windowpanes while you're wrapped up in a warm blanket. I used to have a cat, a big fluffy Maine Coon named Barnaby, who would hide under the bed at the first clap of thunder. He was terrified of loud noises. Even the vacuum cleaner sent him scurrying. I had to buy one of those silent sweepers just to keep the rugs tidy without traumatizing the poor dear...

But to answer your question, no, I've never had that high energy without the other things happening too. They're always a package deal, unfortunately.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I really must insist you get your hearing checked, or perhaps buy a new pen, because we literally just went over this! Are you playing some sort of trick on me? As I said just a moment ago, yes, there was a period of several weeks where I wasn't especially energized or grand at all. My mood was completely fine. But I still heard the whispers in my apartment, and I remained entirely convinced those arts people were monitoring my phone. 

Speaking of phones, did you know they don't even make rotary phones anymore? I used to have a beautiful avocado green rotary phone mounted on the wall in my kitchen. It had such a satisfying heft to the receiver. You could really slam it down if a telemarketer was being rude. Now it's all just tapping on pieces of glass. My niece bought me one of those smartphones, and the screen is always covered in smudges. I try to wipe it with my microfiber cloth—the yellow one, mind you, not the blue one. The blue one is strictly for dusting the porcelain figurines. I have a lovely collection of Lladro figurines in my sitting room. The little girl holding the basket of spring flowers is my absolute favorite. I bought her at an estate sale back in, oh, it must have been 1988. The woman running the sale was wearing the most dreadful floral muumuu, it looked exactly like a couch from the 1970s... 

But honestly, doctor, please write it down this time. Several weeks. No mood issues. Still hearing the whispers and knowing the arts people were on the phone. Do you have it now?

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I am genuinely starting to wonder if you are listening to a single word I say. We have gone over this three times now! Are you writing any of this down? You're looking right at me, but I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, has a brick wall in her backyard, right along the property line. It’s covered in ivy. English ivy, I believe. It looks very picturesque in the spring, but it is an absolute nightmare to maintain. The roots dig right into the mortar and ruin the structural integrity. I told her, "Mildred, that ivy is going to pull your wall down one day," but she just waved me off. She’s terribly stubborn, Mildred is. She insists on wearing open-toed sandals well into November, even when there's frost on the ground. I suppose some people just refuse to listen to reason, much like you refusing to remember what I just told you!

But fine, I will say it one more time, and please, I beg of you, commit it to memory. Yes, there was a period of several weeks where I felt completely normal—not grand, not overly energized, just my regular self. But during that time, the whispers in my apartment were still there, clear as day, and I was still absolutely certain that those arts people were monitoring my phone calls. I don't know how else to explain it to you, doctor. Do I need to write it on a sticky note and put it on your forehead?
